rationale: A wins because it keeps its feet on the supplied facts and does not ask an invented market thesis to carry the business angle. B's line, "The prevailing belief: resale and repair cannibalize new-product sales, so retailers keep them as side projects," is the expensive mistake: that premise is not in the update. A's "REI's record payout to members lands as workers organize" is uncomfortable, but it correctly treats the labor story as a defensive-comment problem before anyone starts pitching sunshine. B has good bones, but one unsupported contrarian frame is enough to make a founder walk into traffic.
gaps_in_A: "REI's record payout to members lands as workers organize" is useful, but placing it with the kept angles risks confusing a defensive prep item with something REI should pitch. The copy says not to pitch it, but the taxonomy still muddies the room.
"A retailer that answers to members rather than a stock price" is fair as structure, but the angle needs to avoid implying the co-op model caused the resale rollout without evidence.

"Your old tent now has a trade-in price at the local REI" is vivid, but tent eligibility and pricing are not in the update. The proof section catches it, but the headline still promises a detail not yet proven.
gaps_in_B: "The prevailing belief: resale and repair cannibalize new-product sales, so retailers keep them as side projects" is invented context. A contrarian angle cannot borrow its enemy from thin air.
"betting on used gear" overstates the facts when the update explicitly says the share of sales from used gear was not disclosed.
"no public shareholders demanding quarterly margin" is an inference from co-op status, not a supplied fact. Fine as a question, sloppy as explanatory color.
"Record dividend lands amid union drives — what REI owes its workers vs its members" is not "off-beat." It is a real labor-risk frame that belongs in defensive prep, not a dismissed refuse pile.
